Pre-AI-boom, Intel was a failing chipmaker. The situation was bad in all respects. Processor design fell behind AMD. Fabs fell behind TSMC/Samsung/etc. Culture was broken. Massive braindrain. Stock was down three-fold between its peak around 2019 and its bottom in 2024/2025. Indeed, it was down three-fold in 2024/2025 from its 2000 dot-com peak. Basically, imploding company, on its way for collapse. With AI boom, there was more demand for ICs than production capacity. It almost didn't matter how bad your chips were -- someone would buy them, and at a healthy markup. This placed Intel in a very strong position to recover. That recovered some value. However, it's worth remembering the peak of $120 was less than double it's dot-com peak 25 years prior. Compare to S&P500 returns or inflation, in an industry otherwise with massive growth. If AI boom doesn't materialize, Intel may, again, be on a path to death. If it does materialize, but like the dot-com boom with a few winners and many losers, Intel will likely be one of the losers. Ergo, falling value. NVidia, in contrast, looks a lot more like the Amazon of the dot-com bust.

This op-ed is horrifically written. > Once you have used a washing machine, laundering clothes by hand seems irrational, even if it might be cheaper. Washing clothes by machine is orders of magnitude cheaper than by hand when you factor in the value of your time. > After you have experienced streaming television, waiting to see a show at a prescribed hour seems silly, even a little undignified. Undignified? What? Completely incoherent word slop. Good to see LLMs haven't completely taken that domain for themselves, I guess - a little hand-crafted slop now and then is a treat, I guess? Anyways, they're wrong. People still tune in to watch scheduled live events all the time. > To resist convenience — not to own a cellphone, not to use Google Neither of these things are a matter of convenience. A cellphone is at this point literally required to participate in a modern economy. Google is a tool that provides you with globally-retrieved information that you otherwise literally could not find on your own or without another similar tool. I don't even disagree with the premise that convenience is a driving factor of our lives, but the justifications and conclusions drawn by this article are beyond stupid. Here's my view of it: the desire for convenience is what pushes us onwards as a species. Hunting for food is inconvenient, so we invented agriculture. Going down to the river or well for water is inconvenient, so we invented indoor plumbing. Repeat ad infinitum until we have modern civilization. There is one part the pessimistic view overlooks; that to achieve maximum convenience long-term requires more effort in the short-term. Developing the skill of programming is inconvenient in the short-term but convenient in the long-term because of the possibilities this opens up to you. This remains true even in the current LLM era, and it will remain true for as long as we are not replaced wholesale by LLMs.

I have what I like to call a semiphotographic memory. I can abstractly remember the positions, shapes, colors and numbers of things extremely well. I can remember sequences of words very well. I can strongly associate it with sensory memories. But I have some weaknesses with it, like temporal trouble. It's hard to natively remember dates and sequences of events. I can strongly remember what the pieced together moments were like, but it's difficult to recall "Did that happen before X or Y?" With things like that I need to remember, I visualize a timeline or a graph in my head or draw it out and take a mental snapshot of that. I've also found that's why I'm a "visual" person when it comes to things like project management. I've imagined a lot of memory management for others must be like that: You find your innate abilities of mental organization, and use it to map the world outside to the world inside. I imagine it looks very different for everyone.
